nameStory: The 'great' in great willowherb refers to its impressive size compared to other willowherbs - it's the tallest member of its family! The 'willowherb' name comes from its narrow, willow-like leaves and its traditional use as an herb for medicinal purposes. Some old-timers still call it 'codlins and cream' after its creamy pink flowers that reminded people of a popular apple dessert.
description: Great willowherb is a tall, robust perennial that can tower up to 6 feet high, making it hard to miss in wetland areas. It produces showy pink to magenta flowers in summer that bloom along tall spikes, each flower having four rounded petals arranged in a cross pattern. The plant has a bushy, upright growth habit with numerous stems branching from the base. Its willow-like leaves are arranged in pairs along the stems, giving the whole plant a lush, leafy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four-petaled pink to magenta flowers about an inch across, arranged in showy terminal spikes. Each petal is deeply notched at the tip, creating a heart-shaped appearance, and the flowers have a sweet, honey-like fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel slightly fuzzy to the touch and have finely toothed edges that you can feel by running your finger along the margin.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and robust, often 4-6 feet high, with multiple stems forming dense colonies. The plant has a distinctly upright, bushy appearance that stands well above surrounding vegetation.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods that split open to release fluffy, white seeds that drift on the wind like tiny parachutes. The pods make a subtle rattling sound when dry and shaken.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, green to reddish stems covered in soft hairs that give them a fuzzy texture when touched. The stems are quite strong and don't break easily when bent.

habitat: Great willowherb thrives in wet soils along streams, pond edges, ditches, and marshes throughout New England. It prefers full sun to partial shade and rich, moist soil, often forming large colonies in disturbed wetland areas. You'll commonly find it growing alongside cattails, purple loosestrife, and other moisture-loving plants in low-lying areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground roots, with fuzzy green stems and opposite leaves beginning to appear in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, with showy pink flower spikes attracting bees and butterflies. This is the best time for identification when flowers are most prominent.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and long seed pods develop, eventually splitting to release fluffy white seeds that drift on autumn breezes. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: The plant dies back to ground level, leaving only dried brown stems and empty seed pods as evidence of its presence.

funFact: Great willowherb is sometimes called 'fireweed' because it's one of the first plants to colonize areas after fires or other disturbances, and a single plant can produce over 80,000 tiny parachute seeds in one season that can travel for miles on the wind!
confusionNotes: Great willowherb is most often confused with purple loosestrife, which also grows in wet areas with pink-purple flower spikes. Remember: willowherb has four-petaled flowers with heart-shaped petals and opposite leaves, while loosestrife has six-petaled flowers and leaves in groups of three. Think 'four-heart willowherb' versus 'six-pack loosestrife.'
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the more famous 'fireweed' (Chamaenerion angustifolium), which is actually a close relative but has different flower arrangements. Great willowherb is native to Europe but has naturalized widely in North America, though it's less aggressive than some other wetland invaders.
compareHints: Among New England's willowherbs, great willowherb lives up to its name by being the tallest and most robust. While cinnamon willowherb has tiny pinkish flowers and fringed willowherb has small white blooms, great willowherb boasts the showiest flowers - large, bright pink, and arranged in impressive terminal spikes. Its fuzzy stems and substantial height make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's willowherbs, cinnamon willowherb is distinguished by its colorful stems and leaves - most other willowherbs stay green throughout the season.
Among New England's willowherbs, fringed willowherb is distinguished by those characteristic tiny hairs along its leaf edges - no other local willowherb has this feature.
Unlike its lowland cousins like great willowherb or cinnamon willowherb, Hornemann's willowherb is much smaller in all respects - shorter stems, tinier flowers, and narrower leaves.
Among New England's willowherbs, linear-leaf willowherb has the narrowest leaves and prefers the wettest habitats.
Among New England's willowherbs, downy willowherb is distinguished by its thoroughly fuzzy texture - much more so than cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb.

Among New England willowherbs, hoary willowherb stands out for its overall grayish, densely fuzzy appearance - most other willowherbs like cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb are greener with less conspicuous hairs.
Marsh willowherb is much smaller and more delicate than Great Willowherb, which can tower over 6 feet tall with showy magenta flowers.
